title: unsafe, pointers, and fixed
hook: `unsafe` does not mean evil. It means the CLR will not verify your pointer arithmetic. Most workers should never enter that context.

sections.heading: What unsafe actually unlocks
sections.prose: In an `unsafe` context you may declare pointers (`int*`, `byte*`), take addresses, and use `stackalloc` as a pointer instead of a `Span`. Function pointers (`delegate*`) call with `calli` instead of allocating a `Delegate`. The project must set `AllowUnsafeBlocks`. None of this is required to slice a CSV or to pass a `Span` into a library. Prefer `Span<T>`, `MemoryMarshal.GetReference`, and `Unsafe` (the `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe` type) helpers that stay in verifiable C# when they can. C# 13 lets iterators contain unsafe regions, but `yield return` must stay in safe code. That is a niche library feature, not a reason to sprinkle `unsafe` in an SQS consumer.

snippets.label: Prefer Span; isolate pointers
snippets.explanation: The foreach version is the default. The pointer version exists to discuss fixed, not to ship in a worker without a profiler saying the JIT lost.

sections.heading: fixed pins against the GC
sections.prose: The GC moves objects. A raw pointer to an array element is invalid the moment a compacting collection runs. `fixed (byte* p = buffer)` pins that object for the statement body. Pinning too long fragments the heap — module 14 territory. `fixed` on a `Span` is legal, but Microsoft’s unsafe best practices forbid passing that pointer across P/Invoke as if it were a null-terminated C string. Spans are not null-terminated; pass an explicit length. Strings are null-terminated; if the native API only takes `wchar_t*`, convert to `string` first or pass length. Do not store the pointer after the `fixed` block.

snippets.label: Length with the pointer
snippets.explanation: Two pins, explicit length, no assumption of a trailing zero. That is the entire safe story for a synchronous native hash.

sections.heading: Interview posture
sections.prose: Say you can read pointer code. Say you enable `AllowUnsafeBlocks` only in the interop project, not in the domain project. Say you would rather wrap SkiaSharp (or any native renderer) in `using` than pin bitmaps by hand. If the interviewer pushes micro-optimization, ask for a trace — `unsafe` without evidence is a reliability regression, not seniority.

interviewTakeaways: unsafe is unverifiable pointer code; AllowUnsafeBlocks is a project-level opt-in.
fixed pins so the GC cannot move the object; do not leak the pointer out of the block.
Never treat a pinned Span as a null-terminated C string; pass length.
commonPitfalls: Keeping a pointer after fixed ends — use-after-free when the GC moves the array.
Enabling AllowUnsafeBlocks on the whole solution because one P/Invoke needed it.
Pointer arithmetic past Length — the runtime will not save you.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS does not expose interior pointers into a GC object. Node addons use N-API and ArrayBuffer backing stores instead of C# fixed.
